title: Mabel and the Sleepy Yawn-Clouds
markdown:
Mabel had fur the colour of perfectly toasted marshmallows and a spirit as bubbly as a fizzy lemonade. She loved to swing from vines with a joyful whoop, chatter with the brightly plumed parrots about the latest jungle gossip, and discover the juiciest sun-ripened mangoes hidden amongst the leaves. But there was one thing Mabel found very, very difficult: settling down. Her little monkey brain was always whirring, like a busy hummingbird’s wings.

As the sun began its slow descent, painting the sky in glorious shades of apricot and rose, the jungle would start to quieten. The boisterous daytime chatter, the squawks and rustles and playful roars, faded into a soft symphony. The gentle chirping of crickets tuned up for their evening performance, and the leaves on the ancient trees whispered secrets to the passing breeze. All the other little creatures, from the sleepy sloths to the busy ants, would find their cozy spots, tucking themselves in, ready for the sweet embrace of sleep. But not Mabel. Mabel would feel a familiar tickle in her toes, a mischievous wiggle in her fingers, and a persistent hum in her tummy that always seemed to say, “More. More adventure. There’s still so much to see.”

She would try, oh, she would try to lie down on her soft mossy bed. She’d close her eyes, but her thoughts would race like tiny excited beetles skittering across a sun-warmed stone. Did I really see that rainbow-coloured butterfly with wings like stained glass? What was that funny fleeting shadow I just glimpsed? I wonder, just wonder, if there are more of those plump red berries just over that whispering hill. And so, with a flick of her tail and a determined glint in her eye, Mabel would leap up again. She’d be off, swinging through the darkening trees in a blur of brown fur, while the world around her, like a contented sigh, drifted into dreams.

In a hidden hollow, nestled amongst the gentlest deepest ferns that smelled like damp earth and moonlight, lived a unique and peaceful dragon named Snuzzle. Snuzzle was not a fire-breathing dragon, goodness no. He would not scorch a single leaf, nor frighten a single firefly. His scales were the colour of the softest deepest moss, and his wings shimmered with the hushed beautiful hues of twilight, like painted silk. Snuzzle’s magic was a quiet gentle magic, a magic of calm and slumber, a magic that smelled of good dreams. When he breathed out, it was not smoke, but tiny wispy clouds that floated through the air, smelling faintly of lavender fields and warm creamy milk. These were sleepy yawn-clouds, collected from the very best sighs of contented creatures.

One evening, as Mabel bounced restlessly from vine to vine, letting out little sighs of frustration that sounded like tiny deflating balloons, Snuzzle peeked out from his ferny hollow. He saw Mabel, a whirlwind of energy against the darkening sky, his soft moss-green dragon eyes full of gentle understanding. “Ah, little one,” he whispered, his voice like the whisper of wind through the reeds by the quiet river, “you seem to have a lot of bouncing in you tonight. Your energy is quite… bubbly.”

Mabel swung down to a lower branch, her little monkey brow furrowed like a worried caterpillar. “I can’t stop, Snuzzle. My feet just won’t stay put. They have wiggles. My hands have wiggles. Everyone else is sleeping, their snores are like little lullabies, but I’m still awake and buzzing like a bee trapped in a jam jar.”

Snuzzle glided over, his twilight-coloured wings making a soft shushing sound, like turning the pages of a quiet book. “There are many ways to find rest, Mabel,” he explained softly. “Sometimes, you just need to learn how to gather the quiet. You can’t always chase it; sometimes, it comes to you when you invite it.” He then did something quite remarkable, something that made Mabel pause her ceaseless bouncing. He took a deep slow breath, filling his small dragon lungs with the calm of the evening air. And then he puffed out a perfect fluffy yawn-cloud. It floated gently, shimmering with pale moonlight and the faintest hint of stardust. “A sleepy yawn-cloud,” Snuzzle explained, his voice as soothing as a mother’s hum, “holds the very essence of a deep peaceful sigh, the feeling of your shoulders relaxing after a long day of play. When you are ready to be calm, you can try to collect one.”

Mabel watched, her usual chattering momentarily stilled. Her bright monkey eyes were wide with curiosity. She had never seen anything like it. Snuzzle gently nudged a yawn-cloud towards her with his smooth mossy nose. It floated closer, tickling her whiskers with its gentle scent and smelling ever so peaceful, like a slumbering meadow. Tentatively, Mabel reached out a small quick hand, and with a soft involuntary sigh, she scooped the cloud into her palm. It felt like holding captured moonlight and the softest warmest down from a swan’s breast. As she brought it closer, the air around her seemed to hum with a gentle quietness, and a wonderful spreading warmth spread through her, a feeling of deep calm she had not realized she was missing. Her restless wiggles began to slow. Her racing thoughts, the ones that bounced from one idea to the next like a pinball, grew still. It felt… lovely. It felt like coming home.

She took another deep breath, a breath that was not rushed or hurried, and another small contented sigh escaped her. Poof. Another tiny yawn-cloud appeared, this one even closer, hovering right in front of her nose. Mabel scooped it up too, her fingers now moving with a new gentleness. She sat there, on the sturdy branch, cradling the two sleepy clouds, her wiggles finally slowing. She listened to the crickets, and for the very first time, their chirping did not sound like a noisy interruption, but like a soothing rhythmic lullaby. She watched the gentle sway of the trees, and it looked not like an invitation to climb, but like a slow peaceful dance.

As Mabel sat there, breathing in the calm of her collected yawn-clouds, her eyelids grew heavy. They felt like little velvet curtains wanting to close. She yawned, a big genuine yawn that stretched her little monkey mouth wide and brought a third, even fluffier cloud right to her waiting palm. She cuddled them close, these little pockets of peace, and as the first bright stars began to twinkle like scattered diamonds in the inky velvet sky, Mabel the monkey, for the very first time, found a deep peaceful sleep. She dreamed of soft moss and quiet streams.

The curious thing about finding peace is this: it is not always about chasing after it with all your might, like trying to catch a slippery fish. Sometimes it is about learning to welcome it in, to make a quiet space for it to settle. Mabel learned that even a restless monkey could find the quiet, not by stopping her wiggles altogether, but by learning to gather the calm, one sleepy yawn-cloud at a time. And she always remembered Snuzzle, the gentle dragon with twilight wings, who taught her the quiet magic of a good deep sigh and the beauty of simply being still.
